lessons.title: The critic's job: review, scholarship and appreciation
lessons.explanation: Criticism is a family of practices with different jobs, different audiences and different standards of evidence, and most confused arguments about literature are confusions about which job is being done. Three members of the family can be distinguished with public-domain examples. A review is a timely assessment of a new work addressed to a reading public; it is bounded by time and space, and its verdict is its product. Poe's 1842 review of Hawthorne shows the constraint openly: having praised the book, he closes, ‘We only regret that the limits of our Magazine will not permit us to pay him that full tribute of commendation, which, under other circumstances, we should be so eager to pay.’ Scholarship works on documents and contexts: establishing what a text is, what its sources are, what a word meant when it was written, and where a passage is disputed — the kind of work that produces an edition you can quote from. Criticism proper, in Samuel Johnson's sense, moves between particular judgements and general principles, and Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare does this in two moves side by side. He argues a general law, ‘Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature’, and then names faults without flinching: ‘He sacrifices virtue to convenience, and is so much more careful to please than to instruct, that he seems to write without any moral purpose.’ Appreciation is the fourth activity, less concerned with verdict or with evidence than with making value perceptible, and Matthew Arnold's theoretical statement of criticism's function is a useful boundary marker because it sets criticism a task beyond judging: ‘It is the business of the critical power’, he writes, quoting his own earlier words, ‘in all branches of knowledge, theology, philosophy, history, art, science, to see the object as in itself it really is.’ Learning to hear which of these four registers a piece of writing is in, and then holding it to that register's standard, is the skill this lesson teaches [1][2][3].
lessons.example: Take Johnson's Preface and separate the operations, because it does four of the four jobs in a single document. First, scholarly groundwork: he establishes which text he is discussing, notes that Shakespeare's plays exist in variant early printings, and refuses to treat corruptions as Shakespeare's design, which is editorial reasoning. Second, general criticism: the law about ‘just representations of general nature’ is a claim about why works endure, and it is contestable — a reader could argue that difficulty and minority taste also survive, and that durability measures institutions as much as nature. Third, particular evaluation: Johnson judges Shakespeare's faults by the same law he has just stated, so his criticism is internally consistent rather than a list of likes. Fourth, appreciation: he also writes with evident pleasure about qualities he admires, and this is where the tone rises. Now apply the same separation to Poe and Arnold. Poe is writing a review and his obligations are to timeliness and a verdict, so his judgement is unavoidably compressed; asking Poe's review for the comprehensiveness of Johnson's Preface would be a category error, and asking Johnson's Preface for Poe's immediacy would be equally unfair. Arnold is not judging any particular work in the passage quoted; he is arguing about what criticism is for, so his claims are about the institution of criticism and should be tested against the practice of critics. When you disagree with a critic, the first question is which register they are working in, because each register has a different failure mode: a review fails by being stale or merely tasteful, scholarship by being inaccurate, and appreciation by being unarguable [1][2][3].
lessons.question: A journalist's verdict on a novel published last month is quoted as though it settled what the novel means. What is the precise problem with the reasoning?
lessons.answer: The quotation moves a timely evaluative judgement into the register of interpretive evidence, so it is being used to prove something it was never designed to establish
lessons.distractor: Journalists lack the qualifications of scholars, so their opinions should never be cited in an argument
lessons.correction: The problem is not the writer's competence but the register's scope. A review's authority concerns its assessment of value and its timeliness, and a claim about meaning needs textual evidence and an argument, which a short review is not built to supply. Citing the review as a voice in the debate is legitimate; citing it as proof is not.

depth.definitions: A review is timely evaluative journalism. Scholarship establishes texts, sources, dates and contexts. Practical criticism (I. A. Richards's term, not used here as authority) attends to the words on the page. Appreciation makes value perceptible. The intentional fallacy is the error of treating an author's stated purpose as decisive about a text's meaning. The affective fallacy is the related error of treating a reader's emotional response as evidence of a work's properties. Prerequisites: the difference between claim and topic from lesson 50, and the standards for an evidential reading set out in lesson 40.
depth.mechanism: Each register determines what counts as support. A reviewer may reasonably rely on a single reading and on their own response, because the audience wants a decision before Thursday; a scholar must show provenance, since a quotation from a corrupt text is a false report; a critic making a general claim must expose the principle behind each judgement so it can be tested against other works. Three consequences matter for a student. First, quoting a review to establish a text's meaning is a category mistake, not a scandal: the review may still be a useful pointer to what was contested at publication. Second, a critic's authority is not transferable as evidence; Johnson's standing does not make the ‘general nature’ claim true, and it is a claim about reception as much as about writing, so it is empirically vulnerable. Third, criticism has institutional pressures that are part of its meaning — magazine space, editorial lines, prize economies, and the reviewing culture of a moment — which is why a historically informed reading asks not only what a critic said but what they were paid and constrained to say. Provenance is the scholar's standard, and it has immediate consequences for quotation: the same 1842 review survives in more than one transcription, and the two witnesses do not agree at every point, one reading ‘will not permit us’ where another reads ‘will nor permit us’. A quoted sentence is therefore only as sound as the edition behind it, and a writer who wants to argue about that sentence should say which witness is being followed, which is a piece of scholarly housekeeping that makes an interpretation harder to dismiss [3]. The limitation of this taxonomy is that real documents mix registers, as Johnson's Preface does, so the tool is for identifying which operation is being performed in a given paragraph, not for sorting writers into boxes [1][2][3].
depth.secondExample: Test the taxonomy on a case where the registers collide. Suppose a modern edition's introduction argues that a poem's meaning depends on a word's eighteenth-century sense. The claim is scholarly because it rests on lexical evidence, but its conclusion is interpretive because it changes what the poem says, and the scholarly part can be checked in a dictionary of the period while the interpretive part must be argued against rival readings of the poem. A reader who disproves the lexical claim has damaged the interpretation; a reader who merely prefers another reading has not. Compare that with an appreciative essay that never makes a checkable claim: it may be valuable and it may be unanswerable, and a reader should notice that these are different achievements. Finally consider the case of an author's own statement of purpose, which this course treats as evidence about the author. Gilman's account of why she wrote her story will help you understand a moment in American medicine; it does not by itself establish what the story does, because the text exists as a set of words that readers can contest. Knowing that an author intended one reading does not prove that the words deliver it, and this is the caution the next two lessons depend on.
depth.mistake: The most frequent error in student argument is treating any printed judgement as an authority whose pronouncement ends a question — ‘Johnson says Shakespeare lacks moral purpose, therefore he does’. Johnson has offered a claim with a stated basis, and the basis can be assessed against the plays. The mirror error is dismissing reviews entirely as journalism, which throws away the best evidence we have about what a work looked like when it first appeared, since a review records contemporary expectations, prices, genres and quarrels that later scholarship must reconstruct. A third error is quieter: mistaking appreciation for criticism and therefore supposing that an unargued preference counts as an interpretive claim. It does not, and a reader who wants to change minds must move from ‘this moves me’ to a statement about what in the text produces the effect, which is again a claim with evidence.
depth.application: Find four pieces of writing about one work: a magazine review, a scholarly article or edition introduction, a critical essay making a general argument, and an appreciative piece. Label each by register, then quote one sentence from each and write 60 words per quotation saying what kind of support that sentence requires and whether the piece supplies it. Model response: for a review, a sentence asserting that a novel's ending fails requires the reviewer to have read the whole book and to specify the failure, and many reviews do specify it in a clause; for a critical essay, a general claim such as Johnson's about what pleases long requires evidence about reception, which Johnson largely assumes. Self-review rubric: full marks require correct register labels, an explicit statement of the evidence each quotation needs, and one instance where the writer successfully meets the standard of their register.
depth.summary: Criticism divides into review, scholarship, criticism proper and appreciation, each with its own audience, constraints and standard of evidence. Poe works under magazine limits, Johnson moves between general law and particular fault without inconsistency, and Arnold sets criticism an institutional task rather than a verdict. Using a source in the wrong register is a specific and diagnosable mistake, and the tool protects you when a quotation is offered as proof of meaning because it was printed. The final two lessons turn this discipline inward: one on symbolism that earns its place, and a capstone in which you must defend a reading against the objection that threatens it most.

lessons.title: Symbolism that earns its place: ‘The Whiteness of the Whale’ and the limits of the symbol
lessons.explanation: A symbol is a concrete thing that also carries a wider meaning, and the difference between a symbol that earns its place and one imposed by a reader is evidential rather than a matter of taste. Three tests do most of the work. Does the text build the association through more than one passage, so that the meaning is produced by the writing rather than imported by the reader? Does the text acknowledge and complicate the association, or does it ignore the counter-evidence? Does the reading account for passages that resist it, or must it select only the convenient ones? Herman Melville's Moby-Dick is an unusually good training text because its narrator performs the first test in public and then demonstrates the second. In chapter 42, ‘The Whiteness of the Whale’, Ishmael assembles white things from a catalogue of dread — the polar bear and the shark (the ‘white-shrouded bear or shark’ whose ghastly whiteness, he says, imparts ‘such an abhorrent mildness, even more loathsome than terrific, to the dumb gloating of their aspect’), the albatross, the pallor of death — and then states the puzzle rather than the solution: ‘But not yet have we solved the incantation of this whiteness, and learned why it appeals with such power to the soul; and more strange and far more portentous — why … it is at once the most meaning symbol of spiritual things, nay, the very veil of the Christian's Deity; and yet should be as it is, the intensifying agent in things the most appalling to mankind.’ He goes on to offer competing explanations as questions — whether whiteness ‘shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and thus stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation’ — and then a harsher image: ‘the palsied universe lies before us a leper’. The chapter therefore models the honest symbol: the meaning is built by accumulation, and the text itself refuses to close it [1].
lessons.example: Run the three tests on the claim that Moby Dick is a symbol of God, and notice how the tests redistribute the burden of proof. Test one, accumulation: the whale recurs across the book — the White Whale is named early, the chapter on its whiteness is preceded by the chapter on Moby Dick himself, and whiteness recurs in the squid, the albatross and the polar bear. The association is therefore not invented by a reader; it is manufactured by repetition across chapters, and any interpretation must begin from that fact. Test two, complication: Ishmael explicitly refuses a settled meaning, offering a list of possibilities in the form of questions, and he attaches the symbol at once to the Christian deity and to annihilation, which means a reading that settles on one of these must explain why the text multiplies. Test three, resistance: the novel also contains long stretches of cetology, of the practical labour of whaling, and of Ahab's personal grievance, and these passages are only weakly illuminated by a theological reading; a good interpretation must say what they are doing rather than waving them away. A stronger claim emerges as a result. Instead of ‘the whale means God’, one might argue that the whale functions as an object that defeats interpretation, and that the novel's method is to load it with incompatible meanings until the act of reading becomes the subject. That claim is checkable: it predicts that the cetology chapters and the legend-collecting chapters are essential rather than digressive, and it names evidence that would damage it, namely a passage in which the narrator settles the whale's meaning and stops generating alternatives [1].
lessons.question: A reader claims the sea in a novel stands for freedom because the characters sail when they feel constrained. Which additional evidence would most strengthen the claim?
lessons.answer: The text returns to the association at other points and also shows the sea constraining a character, so the meaning is built by the writing and complicated by it
lessons.distractor: The author once described the sea in an interview as the freest thing he knew
lessons.correction: The author's remark is evidence about the author's ideas and is famously weak evidence about the work's meaning. The stronger support is internal and repeatable: recurrence establishes that the connection is produced by the text, and an instance of constraining sea shows the association is not a reader's convenience.

depth.definitions: A symbol is a concrete particular that also carries a wider significance; an allegory is a work whose parts systematically correspond to another order of meaning; a motif is a repeated element that may or may not be symbolic. Over-reading is the assignment of significance without textual warrant. Under-reading is refusing a warranted association because it seems too obvious. Prerequisites: the symbol and over-reading lesson from lesson 40, the close-reading method from lesson 37, and the critic's registers from lesson 58.
depth.mechanism: Symbolism works through recurrence, context and contrast, and it is produced rather than detected. Recurrence does the work of a claim inside the text: a word, object or colour that returns across separated scenes has been marked by the author as available for significance, and the reader's task is to ask what the returns have in common. Context governs which meaning survives: the same white whale could mean purity in a devotional poem, and Melville supplies the surrounding catalogue of white horrors precisely so that a naive reading becomes untenable. Contrast fixes range: a symbol is legible mainly against what it is not, so the whiteness matters because the novel also gives blackness, tar, soot and shadow their own associations. Two limits need stating. First, symbols are indeterminate by design; where a text proliferates meanings, an interpretation that forces a single one has smuggled in a preference. Second, the reader's frameworks matter, and a reading legitimately informed by, say, race or empire can find significance the writer did not consciously intend; the requirement is not that the author intended it but that the text can bear it, which is what the three tests measure [1].
depth.secondExample: Apply the tests to a symbol with a much narrower range. In the same novel, the doubloon nailed to the mast is repeatedly interpreted by different crew members, each reading his own meaning into it, which makes the object an image of interpretation itself; the accumulation is small but the text stages the plurality directly, so a claim about it is unusually easy to evidence. Now take a symbol that readers often over-extend: a recurring storm. A storm may carry judgement, upheaval or mere weather, and the tests separate the cases. If the storm appears once and a character happens to become doubtful that night, the association is a coincidence of proximity and the reader has invented it. If storms recur at moments of decision, if the text names the parallel, and if a calm is placed against them, the association has been built, and then the interesting question becomes what the calm is for. Notice that the tests do not settle which meaning is correct; they establish whether a meaning is supported, which is the distinction between an evidential reading and an unsupported one that this level has been developing since lesson 51.
depth.mistake: Two mistakes are common and they pull in opposite directions. The first is symbolic over-reach: assigning significance to every detail, so that a character's umbrella becomes an emblem of sheltering patriarchy and the reader's ingenuity replaces the text's evidence. The diagnostic is a simple question — does the meaning survive if you delete the detail? If yes, the detail is not carrying it. The second mistake is the refusal of symbols altogether, on the grounds that the text only says what it says. That refusal ignores how literature works: recurrence across chapters is a structural fact and a reader who declines to ask what it produces has abandoned a legitimate tool. The correction is to demand the three tests of every symbolic claim, including your own, and to accept that some symbols are indeterminate and that saying so, with reasons, is a result rather than a cop-out.
depth.application: Choose a recurring object or colour in a text you have read and write a 300-word symbolic claim structured by the three tests: list every recurrence with a location, explain what the text does to complicate the association, and name one passage the symbol does not explain. Model response using whiteness in Moby-Dick: recurrences include the White Whale's naming, the chapter on whiteness, the squid and the polar bear; complication is the narrator's own catalogue of white horrors and his refusal to settle the meaning; resistance comes from the cetology chapters, which the symbolic reading must either absorb or concede. Self-review rubric: full marks require quoted or located recurrences rather than asserted pattern, an explicit acknowledgment of a resisting passage, and one sentence stating what evidence would defeat your claim.
depth.summary: A symbol earns its place when the text builds it through recurrence, contextualises it, and leaves traces that a reading must accommodate. Melville's chapter on whiteness is a laboratory because it performs the accumulation and then refuses to close the meaning, attaching whiteness simultaneously to divinity and to annihilation. The three tests convert symbolic claims from assertions of taste into arguments that can be attacked at named points, and they set up the capstone, where you must not only build a reading but defend it against the objection that threatens it most.

lessons.title: Capstone: defending an interpretation against its strongest objection
lessons.explanation: The capstone is not a new skill but the combination of the level's tools under pressure. Take a reading, state it as a claim, put the strongest available objection to it, and then show how the reading survives, is modified, or fails. Charlotte Perkins Gilman's ‘The Yellow Wallpaper’ is a fit case because the two strongest readings of it are genuinely in tension and the evidence for each is locatable. Reading A: the story is a study of mental collapse produced by a treatment, narrated by a woman whose grip on reality progressively fails, and its ending in which she creeps over her fainting husband — ‘so that I had to creep over him every time!’ — is horror. Reading B: the story is a protest against enforced inactivity, and the narrator's increasing identification with the woman behind the pattern is an escape, not a loss, since her language at the end is the language of liberation: ‘I've got out at last … in spite of you and Jane! And I've pulled off most of the paper, so you can't put me back!’ The strongest objection to Reading B is textual and serious. The same final pages that supply the liberation language also supply confinement within a fantasy — ‘I am securely fastened now by my well-hidden rope’ — and a diminished world: ‘I don't want to go outside’, because ‘outside you have to creep on the ground’. A reading that treats the ending as straightforward triumph must explain away its own best quotation's neighbours. The strongest objection to Reading A is equally concrete: the narrator's opposition to her treatment is stated in full, unambiguously and early — ‘Personally, I disagree with their ideas. Personally, I believe that congenial work, with excitement and change, would do me good’ — and her husband's complacent authority is exhibited in a single famous line, ‘John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage.’ A reading that sees only illness must explain why the text gives the diagnosis a named cause [1][2][3].
lessons.example: Build the synthesis and then test it, because a capstone paragraph that only concedes is not an argument. Claim: the story represents the narrator's breakdown as produced by her treatment, so that the cure and the collapse are the same event, and the ending is a liberation that is also a defeat, which is why the writing refuses to choose between the two vocabularies. Evidence for the causal half: the diagnosis is quoted and then contradicted by the patient in consecutive sentences, and the prohibition on work is named as the specific deprivation. Evidence for the ambivalent half: the two endings' quotations above, which juxtapose escape from the paper with a fixed rope and a shrinking outdoor world. Now run the strongest objection against the claim. Objection: this synthesis is unfalsifiable, because any text that mixes triumph and confinement can be described as refusing to choose, and a reading that cannot be wrong is not doing work. Answer it in four moves. Move one, accept the risk and specify what would defeat you: if the final pages contained an undisputed recovery — an exit, a coherent conversation, a return to ordinary practice — the claim about collapse would fail, and the story's ending rules that out. Move two, show that the alternative single readings must explain more than yours: Reading A must explain the explicit causal statement about work, and Reading B must explain the rope. Move three, use the author's own document carefully rather than decisively. Gilman's 1913 account states her purpose — ‘It was not intended to drive people crazy, but to save people from being driven crazy, and it worked’ — which is evidence about her aim and about the story's reception, and it supports the protest reading, but it does not by itself settle what the words do, because a text can exceed or complicate its author's purpose. Move four, restate the claim with its scope: the story stages a treatment that manufactures the condition it claims to cure, and presents the resulting release as inseparable from derangement. That formulation is attackable, evidenced, and says what would change the writer's mind [1][2][3].
lessons.question: A student defends a reading with the author's own statement of purpose, and an examiner replies that this is not enough. Which reply best captures why the examiner is right, while keeping the author's statement usable?
lessons.answer: The statement is evidence about the author's aim and the work's reception, so it supports a reading but does not establish what the words do, which needs textual evidence the reader can test
lessons.distractor: Authors are unreliable about their own work, so their statements have no evidential value at all
lessons.correction: Both extremes are wrong. Dismissing the statement entirely wastes a real historical document, while treating it as decisive commits the intentional fallacy. The usable position treats it as one kind of evidence with a defined scope, which is why it can support a claim without settling it.

depth.definitions: An objection is the strongest available case against a claim; a concession is the part of it the claim must grant; a rebuttal answers the rest. A falsification condition states what evidence would defeat the claim. The intentional fallacy treats an author's purpose as decisive about meaning; the affective fallacy treats a reader's response as evidence of a work's properties. Prerequisites: lesson 50's essay architecture, lesson 40's warrant requirement, lesson 58's separation of critical registers and lesson 59's tests for a symbolic claim.
depth.mechanism: A defended interpretation differs from a confident one in three structural ways. First, the objection is stated at full strength with its best quotation, not in a weakened form the writer can knock down; a straw objection signals that the reading has not been tested. Second, the writer concedes what must be conceded and re-scopes the claim accordingly, which is what converts a thesis into a defensible one — the move from ‘the ending is a triumph’ to ‘the liberation and the derangement are the same event’. Third, the writer names evidence that would defeat the claim, which is what makes the argument empirical rather than aesthetic. Three limitations constrain the capstone. An interpretation cannot be proved, only supported, so the goal is a reading the text can bear that accounts for more of the evidence than its rivals. Authors' statements are relevant but not decisive, since a text's words exceed any stated purpose. And a synthesis is not automatically superior to a clear single reading: if the both-at-once claim cannot name what would disprove it, the simpler reading is the better argument [1][3].
depth.secondExample: Apply the same procedure to a case from earlier in the level, so the method transfers. Suppose you argue that a translation's choice of a reputation-centred epithet for the Odyssey's hero weakens it. The strongest objection is not ‘translations differ’ but Arnold's: that a version must be judged by whether it is rapid, plain in thought and noble, and that a formal choice may serve those ends even at the cost of a nuance. Faced with that, a good answer concedes the criterion and then shows that the epithet's relocation produces a hero who is known rather than resourceful, which damages the poem's later episodes of disguise and invention. The structure is identical to the Gilman case: state the claim, give the best objection with its own authority, concede the criterion, and re-scope the claim to what the evidence supports. Run the same skeleton on Lamb's adaptation, where the objection is that omissions are intrinsic to the aim, and the answer is to show a specific cost the aim did not require. Three applications of one procedure is what a capstone is for.
depth.mistake: The most damaging error is the weak objection: presenting a rival reading as obviously foolish, so that the defence costs nothing and the argument proves nothing. A variant is to concede everything and call the result balanced, which leaves no claim standing and is not an interpretation. A third is to treat the author's stated purpose, or a critic's verdict, as the trump card that ends the dispute; both are aids, neither is decisive. The correction in all three cases is to hold the claim and the strongest objection in view simultaneously, then ask what specific, locatable evidence distinguishes them — and if no such evidence exists, to say so and reduce the claim until it makes a testable difference.
depth.application: Choose a text from this level and write a 600-word defence of a single interpretation against its strongest objection. Requirements: the objection must be stated with its best quotation; the claim must include one concession; and the final paragraph must name what would falsify it. Model response using lesson 53: claim that Poe's unity of effect is a reading preference rather than a law of form; strongest objection is that uninterrupted reading genuinely does produce effects unavailable to serial reading, evidenced by the structure of suspense in magazines; concession that immediacy is real; falsification condition would be a compressed story that achieves its effect only when read in instalments. Self-review rubric: full marks require a rival reading drawn from an actual critical position rather than invented, at least two located quotations from the primary text, an explicit concession sentence, and a falsification condition that a reader could imagine testing.
depth.summary: The capstone assembles the level: narrative speed and compression, borrowed voices in letters and essays, translation as interpretation, adaptation as medium change, the critic's registers and the tests for a symbol all converge on the single demand that a reading be stated as a claim strong enough to be wrong. Gilman's story shows why that demand is not pedantry, since the two readings it invites are both supported and neither can be dismissed, and the strongest work is done by a re-scoped claim that accounts for the escape language and the rope together. Carry the skeleton forward: claim, best objection, concession, re-scoped claim, falsification condition — applied to whatever text you meet next.

readings.note: Read the story complete, twice if possible. Mark the early statement of disagreement with the treatment, the line about John laughing, the passages about the woman behind the pattern, and the final page in full, including the rope. Public domain in the USA; first published 1892.

Public domain; first published in The Forerunner, October 1913. Treat it as evidence about aim and reception, not as the key to the text.

visual.title: The capstone skeleton applied to ‘The Yellow Wallpaper’
visual.description: A five-step argument diagram in which a liberation reading is confronted by the rope and the shrunken world, conceded, and re-scoped into a claim that names its own falsification condition.
steps: Claim: the treatment manufactures the condition it claims to cure, and the release is inseparable from derangement
Best quotation for the claim: ‘Personally, I disagree with their ideas’ and ‘one expects that in marriage’
Best objection in full: the narrator is confined within a fantasy — ‘securely fastened now by my well-hidden rope’ — and ‘outside you have to creep on the ground’
Concession: the ending is genuinely a collapse, and the reading cannot treat the escape language as unambiguous
Re-scope: the story stages both vocabularies because the cure and the collapse are the same event — ‘I've got out at last … so you can't put me back!’ beside the rope
Author's document used with defined scope: Gilman aimed ‘to save people from being driven crazy’ — evidence about aim and reception
Falsification condition: an ending showing undisputed recovery, an exit, or a coherent return to ordinary practice

questions.prompt: Two public-domain translations of one epic opening render a single adjective as ‘ingenious’ and as ‘for wisdom's various arts renown'd’. A student concludes that no version can be better than another because both are interpretations. What is the flaw in that conclusion?
questions.answer: Interpretations can be argued on evidence, so a rendering that relocates the quality in reputation can be tested against the poem's later episodes of invention and disguise
questions.distractor: The flaw is that one translator is later than the other, so the more recent version is necessarily more accurate
questions.correction: Priority in time is not accuracy. The student's relativism fails because the comparison produces specific, checkable consequences: if the hero is characterised by ingenuity, his fabrications and disguises are central, and the text can be cited for or against that. Plurality of readings does not entail equality of readings.

questions.prompt: A prose retelling of a tragedy adds ‘he thought he heard a voice', and a critic calls the addition a failure to trust the drama. Which response is best supported by the adapter's own preface and by the change of medium?
questions.answer: The addition is a necessary consequence of replacing enacted speech with a mediating narrative voice, so it should be judged against the aim the adapters declared
questions.distractor: The addition is a failure, because a retelling should reproduce the source's effects with the minimum of added material
questions.correction: Minimising additions is not a standard any declared aim sets. In prose there is no actor to whom an utterance can be attributed, so attribution must be supplied; judging the retelling by the preface's aim, an introduction to the stories for young readers, is the standard the adapters themselves invited.

questions.prompt: An essay cites a magazine notice of a novel as proof that the novel is a satire. Which diagnosis fits best, and what use could that notice legitimately have?
questions.answer: It misuses an evaluative verdict as interpretive evidence; the notice remains valuable as a record of what readers of the moment took the novel to be
questions.distractor: It is acceptable, because a published critic of the period has specialist knowledge that a modern reader lacks
questions.correction: Specialist knowledge is not the issue; register is. A short review is built to deliver a timely judgement, not to establish meaning through argument. As a witness to contemporary reception and expectations the notice is good evidence, which is precisely the use that would be legitimate.

questions.prompt: A reader argues that a recurring white animal in a novel symbolises death, citing three appearances. Which single addition would most strengthen the claim's standing as evidence rather than preference?
questions.answer: A passage in which the animal's association is complicated or resisted, together with an account of what the reading does with that passage
questions.distractor: A statement from the author's letters confirming that the animal was intended to suggest death
questions.correction: Authorial intention is evidence about the author's design, not about what the text supports, and it leaves the reading untested against the words. Acknowledging a passage that resists the association demonstrates the reading can accommodate contrary evidence, which is what distinguishes an evidential claim from a preference.

questions.prompt: A student's reading of a story as a protest against a medical treatment is met with the objection that the narrator is plainly delusional by the end. Which defence best meets the objection without abandoning the reading?
questions.answer: Concede that the collapse is real and re-scope the claim so that the treatment is represented as producing the condition it purports to cure
questions.distractor: Deny the objection by arguing that the narrator's derangement is a metaphor rather than an event in the story
questions.correction: Treating a plainly narrated condition as mere metaphor discards evidence to protect a thesis. Conceding the collapse and narrowing the claim to the causal relation between treatment and outcome keeps the reading evidential: the text supplies an explicit contradiction of the diagnosis, and the concession costs the argument less than the denial.

questions.prompt: Two novels both claim to be made of contemporary documents. The first is a single writer's dated entries over a year in one city; the second assembles journals, letters and telegrams from five people across two countries. A student concludes that the second is the more reliable book and the first the more limited. Which assessment best separates what the forms actually do?
questions.answer: The single-record book limits knowledge to one writer's reach and turns the arrival of news into an event, while the assembled book gives the reader a joint knowledge no character can possess
questions.distractor: The single-record book is less reliable because an isolated witness cannot be checked, while the assembled book is trustworthy because its documents corroborate one another
questions.correction: Corroboration is a separate question from knowledge, and conflating them is the error here. Isolation makes a record's limits vivid, since news must reach the writer by rumour or report, but an isolated witness may be perfectly accurate, and a chorus of documents may all share one false assumption. The structural difference is how information is distributed across the text, not a ranking of trustworthiness, and the two books produce different reading experiences for that reason alone.

questions.prompt: A novel's first chapter compresses fifty years of family history into three pages and closes with a single question spoken aloud; a short tale compresses twenty years of a man's life into two sentences and spends all its remaining pages on hypotheses about motive. A student argues that both authors were simply short of space. Which claim better accounts for where the compression falls?
questions.answer: Both use compression to install the conditions their pieces need and then dilate exactly where the pressure lies, whether that is a spoken question, a chain of inference, or an interval deliberately left blank
questions.distractor: Both authors shortened their material because the periodicals and formats they wrote for imposed strict limits on length
questions.correction: Space constraints may well be real, but they cannot explain the pattern, because a page limit would not by itself place the dilation so consistently at the point of maximum pressure. The reliable evidence is functional: in the novel the summarised decades exist to load a single question, and in the tale the omitted interval exists to force the reader into the narrator's speculation. Naming that function is an interpretive claim that can be tested against the texts, whereas citing length only redescribes the size of the work.

questions.prompt: A story omits the funeral of a character who has been central to it, and ends instead with a long paragraph describing snow falling across a landscape while nothing further happens to anyone. A reader objects that the story has no conclusion, and another replies that conclusions are a matter of taste. Using this level's tools, which reply is strongest?
questions.answer: The omission withholds what the characters cannot narrate, and the closing pause substitutes a widening of view for the missing event, so the story concludes in reflection rather than in action
questions.distractor: The story does conclude, because the funeral is implied and any reader can supply it from experience, so the objection rests on a misunderstanding
questions.correction: Reader-supplied content is not the same as something the text does, and offering it as the answer abandons the evidence. The workable defence identifies what actually stands in the event's place: the closing paragraph's repetitions, its widening geography, and its final phrase all convert a private grief into a general condition, and that conversion is the conclusion. The objection is answerable, but only by pointing to what the text supplies, not by appealing to the reader's imagination or to the relativity of taste.

questions.prompt: A student writing an essay on idleness adopts the aphoristic mode, producing twelve independent sentences with no visible speaker and no moment of doubt, but one sentence reports the student's own abandoned retirement and the essay ends unresolved. A tutor says the draft belongs to no form at all. Which correction follows from the two essay shapes studied in this level?
questions.answer: The aphoristic mode excludes the writer's own case and the visible search, so the personal sentence must either move to a form that stages enquiry or be cut
questions.distractor: Aphorisms persuade more effectively than personal writing, so the personal sentence should stay because a named speaker adds authority to the rest
questions.correction: Authority in the aphoristic mode comes from the formulation itself, not from a speaker appearing in the text, which is why Bacon's sentences survive being reordered. Keeping one autobiographical sentence inside a set of free-standing maxims produces a page that has neither the portability of the one form nor the visible movement of the other. The remedy is a decision about mode, after which evidence, voice and the shape of the ending follow consistently, and an unresolved close belongs to the enquiring form rather than to the aphoristic one.

questions.prompt: A reviewer praises one English Odyssey as faithful and dismisses another as padded, on the grounds that the second repeatedly adds words to complete its rhymes. A student then argues that the verse version must be superior because Homer wrote poetry. Which assessment of the whole dispute is best supported by the two public-domain translations and by Arnold's argument about faithfulness?
questions.answer: Faithfulness is plural, so the comparison must name its aim: the prose version can keep sense and sequence while the verse version trades literal sense for rhythm and fill, and each choice can be shown in a named line
questions.distractor: The verse version is superior because Homer is a poet and only verse can preserve the true nature of a poem in another language
questions.correction: The claim that only verse can carry a poem is an assumption, not a finding, and prose translations of epic form a long and defensible tradition with their own aims. Meanwhile the reviewer's word 'padded' begs the question by assuming that sense-for-sense equivalence is the only fidelity. The productive procedure is to specify what each version is trying to keep, name the line where the choice becomes visible, and then judge against that stated aim, which is exactly the move Arnold makes when he insists that the disputed question is what faithfulness consists in.

questions.prompt: Two prose retellings of plays are set beside their stage originals: one of a comedy built on disguise and mistaken identity, one of a tragedy built on a murderer's terror. Asked which loses more, a student says both lose equally because prose has no actors. Which account better explains the difference using the idea of medium affordances?
questions.answer: Performance generates laughter from visible incongruity that a summary must explain and thereby dismantles, whereas tragic intensity survives in reported form because a narrator can name the inner state the stage could only imply
questions.distractor: Comedies depend on plot and tragedies on character, and prose retells plots better than it conveys character
questions.correction: That division does not survive contact with the plays, since both depend on plot and character together, and a prose summary can convey character by reporting it. The sharper account turns on what each medium supplies cheaply: the stage can present two bodies in one space and let an audience see a discrepancy between what a figure claims and what the audience knows, which is the whole mechanism of comic disguise, whereas terror is largely interior and transfers into narration as soon as a voice exists to report it. That difference is a testable claim about the two transfers rather than a preference about genres.

questions.prompt: An essay cites an eighteenth-century critic's general law, that nothing pleases many and pleases long but just representations of general nature, and then treats it as a settled fact about why literature survives. A reader objects that the sentence is doing all the work. Which revision would make the argument sound while keeping the critic usable?
questions.answer: Treat the claim as a contestable proposition about what readers have rewarded, then test it against works whose durability rests on difficulty or on institutions rather than on generality
questions.distractor: Attribute the claim explicitly to the critic, since naming a respected authority transfers that authority to the proposition being quoted
questions.correction: Attribution is not support: a critic's standing is evidence about the critic, not about what has lasted, and the sentence is a generalisation about reception rather than a rule of composition. It becomes usable once it is placed in the register it belongs to, where the history of reading, the survival of difficult and coterie works, and the role of schools and editions in keeping texts alive all count as relevant evidence. That is the difference between citing a critic to end a question and engaging a critic to open one, and it is the discipline the lesson on critical registers asks for.

questions.prompt: One reader argues that a colour repeated across a novel carries the meaning of annihilation, citing three scenes; a second reader argues the same colour carries spiritual or sacred meaning, citing one different scene. A third reader proposes settling the dispute by counting appearances. Using this level's tests for a symbolic claim, what should happen instead?
questions.answer: Both claims should be examined for recurrence and complication, since a text may deliberately attach one image to opposed meanings, and the test is whether each reading can accommodate the passages that resist it
questions.distractor: The claim supported by more scenes should be preferred, because the frequency of an image's occurrence measures the strength of its symbolic meaning
questions.correction: Counting appearances measures prominence, not meaning, and the same novel can load a single image with opposed significance while the text itself refuses to settle it, which is exactly what happens when a narrator catalogues white things and then multiplies explanations for them. The workable procedure treats both readings as claims and asks which one can account for the same evidence, including the passages that inconvenience it. A reading that must ignore a passage is weaker than one that can absorb it, and where neither can absorb the other, the honest conclusion is that the symbol is indeterminate, supported with the reasons why.

questions.prompt: In a diary novel whose entries are written after the events they report, a character's thoughts are recorded in a tone of moral disapproval that does not match the diarist's own expressed attitudes elsewhere in the book. A student labels the narrator unreliable. Which combination of this level's tools best describes what is happening and how the claim should be argued?
questions.answer: Free indirect discourse inside a retrospective record, so the sentence must be assigned by locating markers such as tense, evaluative vocabulary and the diarist's contrary views elsewhere
questions.distractor: An unreliable narrator, diagnosed from the fact that a diary writer cannot accurately report what other people are thinking
questions.correction: Two different questions have been merged. Who is speaking in a sentence is a matter of speech representation, and the mismatch of tone with the diarist's own attitudes is precisely the signal of a character's voice entering the narration, which is a feature of technique rather than a defect of truthfulness. Unreliability concerns the truth of an account and requires evidence of distortion or contradiction plus some sense of the norm being departed from. Diagnosing it from the diary form alone would beg the question, since partiality and a first person are not by themselves grounds for thinking an account false.

questions.prompt: A story is told entirely through dated documents by one narrator whose prose grows more fragmented as the months pass and whose images become steadily more violent, and no second account of the same events is ever supplied. A reader claims the narrator is unreliable, and a second reader replies that the story simply has a disturbed style. Which requirement would turn the first claim into an argument rather than a label, and what does the reply get right?
questions.answer: Evidence within the account of distortion or contradiction, together with a sense of the norm the narrator violates, since a first-person record is not unreliable merely for being partial
questions.distractor: Proof that the narrator is insane, established sufficiently by the story's disturbed imagery and its increasingly broken sentences
questions.correction: A disturbed style may support a reading of instability, but style cannot establish unreliability on its own, because unreliability is a relation between an account and what the text leads a reader to accept. Without a norm the narrator departs from, or a contradiction the text supplies, the label adds nothing to a stylistic description and cannot be argued against. Notice too that the same evidence about fragmentation may be doing a different job, such as registering the pressure of confinement, and a claim that cannot distinguish these possibilities is not yet an interpretation of the story.

questions.prompt: An interpreter supports a reading of a story by quoting the author's account, written twenty years later, of what the story was meant to achieve. An examiner objects, and the interpreter asks whether the document must now be abandoned. If the interpreter wants to keep using it, what is the correct disposition of the evidence?
questions.answer: Retain it as evidence about the author's aim and the work's early reception, and argue the interpretation from the text, since a stated purpose does not establish what the words do
questions.distractor: Discard it, because an author's statements about their own work are categorically inadmissible in interpretation
questions.correction: Categorical exclusion overstates the case and throws away a genuine historical document that can date a controversy, explain a choice and record a book's effects on its first readers. What the document cannot do is settle meaning, because the words of a text exist independently of the purpose behind them and can exceed or complicate it. The disciplined position gives each kind of evidence its proper scope: the account of aim belongs to reception history and authorial intention, while claims about what the story does must rest on textual evidence that another reader can check and contest.

questions.prompt: A student must choose between two readings of one text. The first is simple and can name the evidence that would defeat it. The second accounts for more passages by describing the text as holding two opposed meanings at once, but its author cannot say what would disprove it, on the grounds that any passage can be read as supporting the tension. Which choice, and on what grounds?
questions.answer: The simpler reading, because a claim that cannot specify what would falsify it has abandoned the discipline that makes interpretation arguable, however much ground it covers
questions.distractor: The richer reading, because an interpretation that accounts for more passages is by definition the more complete and therefore the better account
questions.correction: Coverage is a virtue only while the claim remains testable. A reading that absorbs every passage by refusing to commit is compatible with any text at all, which is why it performs no critical work and cannot be refuted by a stronger reader. The criterion is falsifiability joined to coverage, and where the two conflict the claim that can be attacked is the one that can be defended. The student can still honour the second reading's insight by re-scoping it until it makes a difference that could be tested, which is the move the capstone lesson practises.
